RATIÉ CH. 2 — THE RIPOSTE: THE PROBLEM OF COGNITIVE SYNTHESIS

  • er-chapter analysis for the thesis. Source lines 5925–8573. The riposte to the Buddhist
  • -self: the Self is needed for the synthesis of cognitions (memory, recognition across
  • ments).*

1. THE CHAPTER'S THESIS

  • e Buddhist has denied the Self; the Pratyabhijñā shows the Self is *needed for the
  • nthesis of cognitions* — memory and recognition across moments are impossible without a
  • rsisting subject. This is where the felt self emerges.

2. EXTENDED QUOTES (French verbatim + English translation)

Q1 — Memory = asampramosha (no complete dispossession) (lines 6924–6939)

"La forme essentielle (ātmīya) de la mémoire consiste à manifester [quelque chose]
exactement de la même manière [que dans le passé]… le fait qu'il n'y a pas dépossession
complète (asampramoṣa)… de l'objet expérimenté."
**"The essential form (ātmīya) of memory consists in manifesting something exactly in the
same way as in the past — the fact that there is no complete dispossession
(asampramoṣa) of the experienced object."**
  • → Memory = the recovery of what was never truly lost. The template for recognition
  • re-cognition.**

Q2 — Memory as re-appropriation (lines 6973–6981)

"La mémoire est expérience d'une réappropriation de l'objet passé : se souvenir, c'est
réaliser que le passé n'est pas complètement perdu."
**"Memory is the experience of a re-appropriation of the past object: to remember is to
realize that the past is not completely lost."**

Q3 — Synthesis (anusandhāna) = the life of all mundane existence (ĪPK 1.3.6, lines 7409–7424)

"evam anyonyabhinnānām aparasparavedinām / jñānānām anusandhānajanmā naśyej janasthitiḥ
// … l'existence mondaine, qui naît de la synthèse (anusandhāna)… toute activité mondaine
suppose… le désir… le désir suppose à son tour la mémoire (smṛti)."
**"If one accepted [the Buddhist thesis], the mundane existence that arises from the
synthesis (anusandhāna) of cognitions… would have to perish… all mundane activity
presupposes… desire… and desire presupposes memory (smṛti)."**

Q4 — Vimarśa = the felt self-luminous grasping (lines 8134–8150)

"Vimarśa désigne… le fait que la conscience n'est pas seulement manifestation (prakāśa)…
mais en prend conscience… cette saisie immédiate de soi qui constitue la conscience de
soi (svasamvedana)."
**"Vimarśa designates… the fact that consciousness is not merely manifestation (prakāśa)…
but becomes aware of it… this immediate self-seizure that constitutes the self-consciousness
(svasamvedana)."**
  • → Vimarśa = the felt, self-luminous moment of every cognition. The felt substrate
  • at recognition re-appropriates.**

Q5 — Even perception contains a vimarśa (ĪPK 1.5.19, lines 8279–8327)

"sākṣātkārakṣaṇe'py asti vimarśaḥ… Même au moment de la perception immédiate, il y a une
prise de conscience (vimarśa)… d'une manière si subtile que d'ordinaire nous n'y prêtons
pas attention."
**"Even at the moment of immediate perception there is a taking-conscious (vimarśa)… in so
subtle a manner that ordinarily we do not pay attention to it."**
  • → POST-RECOGNITION SEED.** Recognition is not an added construction but the explicit
  • covery of what is always latently felt. The felt is always already there.

Q6 — The synthesis of the anterior and posterior forms of the "I" (lines 8461–8473)

"cette 'synthèse des formes antérieure et postérieure du Je' (aham iti pūrvāpararūpānusandhāna)
par laquelle le sujet percevant se saisit à la fois comme la conscience d'où émerge
l'objet et comme la conscience où il se résorbe."
**"this 'synthesis of the anterior and posterior forms of the I' by which the perceiving
subject seizes itself at once as the consciousness from which the object emerges and as
the consciousness in which it is reabsorbed."**
  • → THE FELT MOTION OF RE-COGNITION.** The self spans its own moments — the felt motion
  • at the paper's post-recognition theory rests on.

Q7 — Cognitions are "blind, deaf and mute" to each other (lines 8511–8562)

"ces cognitions… sont pour ainsi dire inconscientes, aveugles, sourdes et muettes en ce
qui concerne l'objet des autres… la synthèse… ne peut provenir ni de la nature [de chaque
cognition], ni de l'objet."
**"these cognitions… are as it were unconscious, blind, deaf and mute with regard to the
object of the others… the synthesis… can proceed neither from the nature of each
cognition nor from the object."**
  • → No objectified cognition can synthesize others. Only a self that is the felt light
  • all cognitions can effect the re-cognition.** The felt cannot be captured as an object
  • the non-objective felt.

3. IPK LINKS

  • ĪPK 1.3.4 (memory = asampramoṣa) — Q1.
  • ĪPK 1.3.6 (anusandhāna synthesis) — Q3, Q7.
  • ĪPK 1.5.19 (vimarśa in every perception) — Q5, Q6.
  • The synthesis argument → ĪPK 1.3.7 (the unifier, treated in Ch3).

4. THESIS LITERATURE-REVIEW VALUE

  • Memory as re-appropriation (Q1, Q2) = the felt template for recognition.
  • The felt is always already present (Q4, Q5): vimarśa is latent in every perception —
  • cognition makes it explicit. This is the paper's post-recognition re-rendering.
  • The felt is non-objective (Q7): the synthesizing self cannot be objectified. Pairs
  • th Solms' felt-as-non-objective affect.
  • The "synthesis of the anterior/posterior I" (Q6) = the felt spanning of moments —
  • lms' autonoetic memory / the felt-enduring subject.

5. ⭐ THE SVASAMVEDANA DIALECTIC (the deep crux — mined from Ratié Ch2, lines 5925–6254)

  • is is the single most important dialectical passage for the felt-self thesis. Deep-mined
  • om the primary source:
  • The no-self challenge (Ch1, the strongest form):** the trace (saṃskāra) suffices to
  • plain memory; the Self is a "useless burden" (antargaḍu). Ratié notes the Vaiśeṣika's own
  • āvanā is "the cause of souvenir (smṛti) AND recognition (pratyabhijñāna) of objects
  • ready experienced" (lines 4243–4250) — **recognition already appears in the rival system
  • an ordinary byproduct of the trace.**
  • Utpaladeva's riposte (ĪPK 1.3.1, lines 5962–5984):* the trace explains the *object of
  • mory but NOT the felt consciousness that this was experienced by me:
"cette cognition, confinée à elle-même (ātmaniṣṭha), ne peut pas faire connaître
l'expérience originale."
"this cognition, confined to itself, cannot make known the original experience."
  • The Buddhist's reply (lines 6063–6089):* memory takes the past *cognition as its
  • ject ("j'ai perçu la tasse ce matin").
  • The Śaiva's fatal counter (lines 6090–6184):** this contradicts the Buddhist's OWN
  • inciple of svasamvedana (self-awareness). If every cognition is self-aware, it can
  • ver be the object of another — so memory cannot objectify the past experience:
"la cognition est l'acte d'objectivation que rien ne peut à son tour objectiver."
"cognition is the act of objectivation that nothing can in turn objectify."
  • The scholarly crux — the "glissement de sens" (subversion of meaning, lines 6129–6148):**
  • e Śaiva ADOPTS the Buddhist's svasamvedana but SHIFTS its meaning — from "no Self needed"
  • uddhist) to "the felt-self is real, non-objective, and prior to cognition" (Śaiva).
  • The felt-self conclusion:** memory is not object-recall but the felt re-cognition of
  • his was experienced by me" — a felt dimension that the objectifying machinery (the
  • ace) cannot capture. The felt self is real, non-objective, and prior to cognition.
CONNECTION TO SOLMS: the felt is non-objective (cannot be objectified — the Śaiva
proof) = Solms' felt (affect) is non-objective (Ch5). But NOTE the dissonance (see
CRITICAL-COMMENTARY-felt-self-dialectic.md, Dissonance 3): the Buddhist, Śaiva, and
Solms all hold the felt is non-objective, but for INCOMPATIBLE reasons. The convergence
is phenomenological, not metaphysical.

6. IPVV TRANSLATION HOOKS

  • anusandhāna (synthesis) / anusandhātṛ (synthesizer) — the life of cognition.
  • smṛti (memory) / asampramoṣa — memory's essence.
  • vimarśa / svasamvedana — the felt self-grasping.
  • aham iti pūrvāpararūpānusandhāna — the synthesis of the two "I"s.
  • saṃskāra (impression) — the Buddhist rival explanation.
  • h2 is where the felt self emerges: memory is re-appropriation (never truly lost),
  • marśa is latent in every perception, and the synthesizing self is non-objective. This is
  • e paper's foundation for recognition-as-felt and post-recognition re-rendering. The
  • lind, deaf, mute" cognitions (Q7) prove only a felt self can unify them.*
